clinicalPearls: Caused by recessive variants in SGCG encoding gamma-sarcoglycan; historically termed the severe childhood autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy of North African populations.
A recurrent founder deletion in SGCG is particularly common in North African communities, so ancestry and founder-variant testing can shorten the diagnostic pathway.
The phenotype is typically severe and Duchenne-like, with early childhood onset, calf hypertrophy, Gowers sign and often early loss of ambulation.
Serum creatine kinase is very high, in the range associated with dystrophinopathy.
As with the other sarcoglycanopathies, loss of gamma-sarcoglycan usually reduces immunostaining of the whole sarcoglycan complex.
Cardiac involvement occurs but has generally been reported as less consistent than in the beta- and delta-subtypes (LGMD R4 and R6).
Cognition is preserved, which helps separate it clinically from Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
reference.pathophysiology: LGMD R5 results from biallelic pathogenic variants in SGCG on chromosome 13q12, encoding gamma-sarcoglycan, a transmembrane component of the sarcoglycan subcomplex of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex. Like the other sarcoglycans, gamma assembles interdependently with alpha, beta and delta, so a pathogenic change reduces membrane expression of the whole tetramer and disrupts the structural link between the subsarcolemmal cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix. The destabilised sarcolemma is vulnerable to mechanical stress during contraction, producing repetitive fibre necrosis and regeneration, inflammation and progressive fibro-fatty replacement. A specific recurrent founder deletion in SGCG accounts for a large share of cases in North African ancestry populations and typically produces a severe, early-onset phenotype, underpinning the historical designation of this subtype as a severe childhood recessive dystrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy given the severe childhood proximal picture
additionalInvestigations: Targeted testing for the recurrent SGCG founder deletion in patients of relevant ancestry
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for the sarcoglycan complex and dystrophin
SGCG sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis or an LGMD gene panel
Baseline and surveillance echocardiography and pulmonary function testing
redFlags: Early loss of independent walking in childhood
Emerging respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation
New cardiac symptoms or reduced ventricular function on imaging
Rapid scoliosis progression after loss of ambulation
reference.prognosis: The phenotype is frequently severe, and many affected children lose independent ambulation relatively early, broadly resembling the trajectory of dystrophinopathy. Long-term outlook is shaped by progressive respiratory muscle weakness and, less consistently than in beta- or delta-subtypes, by cardiac involvement.
pitfalls: Not testing for the recurrent SGCG founder deletion in patients of North African ancestry, delaying diagnosis
Assuming milder disease by analogy with alpha-sarcoglycanopathy
Mislabelling as Duchenne muscular dystrophy without genetic confirmation
Neglecting scoliosis and respiratory surveillance once a child becomes non-ambulant
references: Peer-reviewed limb-girdle muscular dystrophy classification and consensus statements
